title: Ack timing decides the guarantee
summary: At-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once come down to one question: do you acknowledge before or after the work?

steps.title: Three guarantees, one decision
body: Every broker hands you a message and waits for a signal: an **ack** (RabbitMQ `basic.ack`) or a **committed
offset** (Kafka). Where you put that signal relative to the work decides what happens when the process dies
half-way, and processes always die half-way eventually: a deploy, an OOM kill, a node drain.
```text
receive ──► work ──► ack          crash between work and ack
at-least-once:      ════════════════════════►         → redelivered → work runs TWICE
receive ──► ack ──► work          crash between ack and work
at-most-once:       ════════════════════════►         → broker forgot it → work NEVER runs
"exactly-once":     at-least-once delivery + an effect that is safe to repeat (idempotent)
- **At-most-once** is fine for metrics samples or presence pings, where a gap is cheaper than a duplicate.
- **At-least-once** is the default for anything that matters (orders, payments). Duplicates are certain, so
the consumer must make them harmless. The rest of this module is about how.
- **Exactly-once** is not a delivery mode a network can give you. It is an *end-to-end* property you build.
> **See it:** open **Labs → Messaging builder → Kafka** and play the challenge *Committed, then crashed*, then
> **Labs → Messaging builder → RabbitMQ** and play *Auto-ack ate my order*.

steps.prompt: Which guarantee does each setup give you when the consumer or producer crashes at the worst moment?
items: RabbitMQ: `BasicAckAsync` after the handler committed its database transaction
A producer that retries a send whose ack timed out (no idempotence)
A producer that fires and forgets: no confirms, no retries
explain: With `autoAck: true` RabbitMQ considers the message delivered the moment it is written to the socket: a crash
loses it. Committing before the work is the same mistake in Kafka. Acking after the work, or retrying a send whose
outcome you do not know, always errs on the side of a duplicate.

steps.title: Watch a crash produce a duplicate
body: Kafka's committed offset is "the **next** offset to read". This consumer processes, *then* commits, and crashes
right after charging `m2`. Step through it and watch `committed` and `charged`: the restart begins at the
committed offset, so `m2` is charged a second time. Nothing was lost; something was repeated.

steps.prompt: A RabbitMQ billing consumer acks **after** its database commit. The pod is OOM-killed after the commit but before `BasicAckAsync` reaches the broker. What happens next?
options: The channel closes, the unacked message goes back to the queue and is delivered again with `ea.Redelivered == true`; without an idempotent handler the customer is charged twice
The message is lost, because the database already has the row
RabbitMQ notices the database row and drops the duplicate
The message goes straight to the dead-letter exchange
explain: The broker only knows "delivered, not acked". When the connection drops, every unacked delivery on it is
requeued. `Redelivered` is a hint ("this may have been seen before"), not proof: the first delivery may have
failed before doing anything. So you cannot skip on `Redelivered` alone; you need a dedup key (lesson 3).

steps.title: The producer side duplicates too
body: Duplicates do not only come from consumers. A producer sends, the broker writes the message, and the **ack is
lost** (timeout, connection reset). The producer cannot tell "not written" from "written, ack lost", so it retries:
```text
producer ──send m7──► broker (writes m7)   ✗ ack lost
producer ──retry m7─► broker (writes m7 again)   → two copies in the log
- **Kafka** fixes this one hop with the **idempotent producer**: the broker tracks a producer id and a sequence
number per partition and drops a retried batch it already has. The Java client enables it by default since
Kafka 3.0; **librdkafka and Confluent.Kafka do not**, so set it:
`new ProducerConfig { Acks = Acks.All, EnableIdempotence = true }` (idempotence requires `acks=all`).
- **RabbitMQ** publisher confirms tell you a message is safe, but a confirm lost with the connection means you
republish and the queue may hold two copies. RabbitMQ has no broker-side dedup, so set a stable
`BasicProperties.MessageId` and let consumers dedup.
Either way the rule holds: **exactly-once processing = at-least-once delivery + idempotent handling.**

steps.prompt: Complete the Confluent.Kafka consumer so an offset is stored only after the order has shipped, and the pod leaves the group cleanly on shutdown.
code: using var consumer = new ConsumerBuilder<string, string>(cc).Build();
explain: With `EnableAutoOffsetStore = false` the background auto-commit only commits offsets you explicitly stored, and
you store each one after `Ship` returns. `Close()` commits the stored offsets and leaves the group, so the
rebalance is fast and the next owner starts where you stopped. Skipping `Close` (or getting SIGKILLed) means the
group waits for the session timeout and the new owner redelivers everything after the last commit.

steps.title: Fix the lost shipment
prompt: **Symptom.** Support: "order `o-17` was paid but never shipped". The shipping pod's log:
```text
10:02:11.204 INFO  shipping committed offset 2 (partition orders-0)
10:02:11.207 WARN  container shipping-7f9c restarted: OOMKilled (exit code 137)
10:02:13.880 INFO  shipping resumed at offset 2, shipped o-18
`ShipmentConsumer.Run(log, crashAt)` processes the log from `Committed` to the end. The line
`if (i == crashAt) return false;` simulates the pod dying while it handles record `i` (keep that line **between**
the two actions). `crashAt = -1` means no crash. Calling `Run` again simulates the restart: `Committed` and
`Shipped` survive, like the broker's offset and the real shipments.
Fix the order of the actions so the consumer is **at-least-once**: after a crash on `o-17` and a restart, every
order has shipped (a repeat of `o-17` is acceptable for now; lesson 3 makes it harmless). `Committed` is always
the next offset to read.
starter: public int Committed { get; private set; }
public bool Run(string[] log, int crashAt)
for (int i = Committed; i < log.Length; i++)
if (i == crashAt) return false; // the pod dies here
solution: public int Committed { get; private set; }
public bool Run(string[] log, int crashAt)
for (int i = Committed; i < log.Length; i++)
if (i == crashAt) return false; // the pod dies here
Committed = i + 1;              // then commit the next offset to read
hints: The log says the offset was committed *before* the pod died. Which action has to come first so a crash cannot skip work?
Ship, then the crash check, then `Committed = i + 1`.
template: var dojoLog = new[] { "o-16", "o-17", "o-18" };
var dojoC = new ShipmentConsumer();
Dojo.Eq("first run dies while handling o-17", false, dojoC.Run(dojoLog, 1));
Dojo.Eq("after the crash the committed offset still points at o-17", 1, dojoC.Committed);
Dojo.Eq("the restart runs to the end", true, dojoC.Run(dojoLog, -1));
Dojo.Eq("every order shipped (o-17 twice is the at-least-once price)", new List<string> { "o-16", "o-17", "o-17", "o-18" }, dojoC.Shipped);
Dojo.Eq("committed offset is the log end", 3, dojoC.Committed);
var dojoC2 = new ShipmentConsumer();
Dojo.Eq("no crash: runs to the end", true, dojoC2.Run(dojoLog, -1));
Dojo.Eq("no crash: each order exactly once", new List<string> { "o-16", "o-17", "o-18" }, dojoC2.Shipped);
{{CODE}}
explain: Swapping two lines changes the guarantee from "can lose" to "can duplicate". Losing an order is invisible until a
customer calls; a duplicate can be detected and made harmless. That is why at-least-once is the default.

steps.title: Simulate both guarantees
prompt: Write `string Simulate(string[] log, bool ackAfter, int crashAt)` that replays one crash and reports what it cost.
- **Run 1** starts at offset 0. For each record `i`:
- `ackAfter == true`: process it, then if `i == crashAt` the pod dies, otherwise commit `i + 1`;
- `ackAfter == false`: commit `i + 1`, then if `i == crashAt` the pod dies, otherwise process it.
- **Run 2** (the restart) starts at the committed offset and runs to the end with the same order of actions and no crash.
- `crashAt = -1` means run 1 never crashes.
Return `"processed {list} | duplicates {list} | lost {list}"` where lists are joined with `,` and an empty list is `-`:
- `processed`: every processing in the order it happened;
- `duplicates`: ids processed more than once, in log order, each once;
- `lost`: ids in the log never processed, in log order.
```text
Simulate(["m1","m2","m3"], ackAfter: true,  crashAt: 1)  →  "processed m1,m2,m2,m3 | duplicates m2 | lost -"
Simulate(["m1","m2","m3"], ackAfter: false, crashAt: 1)  →  "processed m1,m3 | duplicates - | lost m2"
starter: string Simulate(string[] log, bool ackAfter, int crashAt)
// run 1 (may crash), then run 2 from the committed offset
solution: string Simulate(string[] log, bool ackAfter, int crashAt)
for (int i = committed; i < log.Length; i++)
string Join(IEnumerable<string> xs) => xs.Any() ? string.Join(",", xs) : "-";
var duplicates = log.Distinct().Where(id => processed.Count(p => p == id) > 1);
hints: Wrap the record loop in `for (int run = 1; run <= 2; run++)` and only crash when `run == 1`.
A crash is a `break` out of the record loop; `committed` keeps whatever value it had.
`log.Distinct().Where(id => processed.Count(p => p == id) > 1)` gives the duplicates in log order.
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoLog = new[] { "m1", "m2", "m3" };
Dojo.Eq("ack after, crash on m2: duplicate", "processed m1,m2,m2,m3 | duplicates m2 | lost -", Simulate(dojoLog, true, 1));
Dojo.Eq("ack before, crash on m2: lost", "processed m1,m3 | duplicates - | lost m2", Simulate(dojoLog, false, 1));
Dojo.Eq("no crash, ack after", "processed m1,m2,m3 | duplicates - | lost -", Simulate(dojoLog, true, -1));
Dojo.Eq("no crash, ack before", "processed m1,m2,m3 | duplicates - | lost -", Simulate(dojoLog, false, -1));
Dojo.Eq("ack after, crash on the last record", "processed m1,m2,m3,m3 | duplicates m3 | lost -", Simulate(dojoLog, true, 2));
Dojo.Eq("ack before, crash on the first record", "processed m2,m3 | duplicates - | lost m1", Simulate(dojoLog, false, 0));
Dojo.Eq("ack before, crash on the last record", "processed m1,m2 | duplicates - | lost m3", Simulate(dojoLog, false, 2));
Dojo.Eq("empty log", "processed - | duplicates - | lost -", Simulate(new string[0], true, -1));
